say: You give it the log of a function, $\ln f(x)$. It gives back the slope function, $f'(x)$ over $f(x)$.
The key idea: the derivative of a log is the **derivative of the inside**, divided by the inside.

how.higher: It turns up as a step inside larger Paper 1 parts, in about one part a year from 2017 to 2025, usually a rate or slope in a word problem, worth 5 to 10 marks.

example.question: Find the slope of the curve $y = \ln(3x^2 + 1)$ at $x = 1$.

steps.title: Name the inside
steps.say: The log has a function inside it. Call the inside $\hl{1}{u}$ and find its derivative.

steps.title: Apply the log rule
steps.say: The derivative of $\ln u$ is $u'$ over $u$. Put $u'$ on top and $\hl{1}{u}$ on the bottom.

steps.title: Put in x = 1
steps.say: The slope at $x = 1$ is the derivative with $1$ in place of $x$.

higher.tip: Write down any differentiation you can. Partial marks go for correct work even if you do not finish.
Differentiate the whole expression before you substitute a value. A fully differentiated expression earns its own credit.
Substitute the value into every term of the derivative, not just some of them.
Give the answer in the form the question asks for. The wrong form loses a mark.

sources.quote: Answer not in the correct form

say: You give it an inverse trig function of $x/a$, like $\tan^{-1}(x/a)$. It gives back the slope function.
The key idea: the rule for $\tan^{-1}u$ is $u'$ over $1 + u^2$, and the chain rule supplies $u'$.

steps.title: Name the inside
steps.say: The inverse trig rule needs the inside. Call it $\hl{1}{u}$ and find $u'$.

steps.title: Apply the rule
steps.say: The derivative of $\tan^{-1}u$ is $u'$ over $1 + u^2$.

say: You give it a function, $f(x)$. It finds the slope function $f'(x)$ using the limit $\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
The key idea: the slope between two points a distance $h$ apart becomes the slope **at** a point when $h$ shrinks to zero.

how.higher: It is a whole Paper 1 part of its own, in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024, always with a linear or quadratic $f(x)$ and worth 10 to 20 marks.

steps.title: Find f(x + h)
steps.say: Replace every $x$ in the function with $x + h$, then multiply out.

steps.title: Subtract f(x)
steps.say: Take away $f(x)$. Every term without an $h$ cancels.

steps.title: Divide by h
steps.say: Every term has an $h$. Divide it out.

steps.title: Let h go to 0
steps.say: Now let $h$ shrink to zero. The $2h$ term disappears.

higher.tip: Use first principles. Any other method of differentiating earns nothing.

sources.quote: No credit if first principles is not used

higher.tip: Write the limit sign on every line until $h$ goes to zero. Leaving it out is penalised.

sources.quote: omission of limit sign penalised once

higher.tip: Start by writing $f(x+h)$. Even this alone earns partial credit.
Show the left-hand side, $f(x+h) - f(x)$ over $h$, as well as the right-hand side.

say: You give it one function divided by another, $u/v$. It gives back the slope function $\dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$.
The key idea: differentiate the top and the bottom separately, then combine them in the fixed pattern: bottom times the top's slope, minus top times the bottom's slope, all over the bottom squared.

how.higher: It is a step inside a Paper 1 part in 2024 and 2025, worth 10 marks each time, either to find a slope at a point or to show a function has no turning points.

steps.title: Name top and bottom
steps.say: Call the top $\hl{1}{u}$ and the bottom $\hl{2}{v}$. Differentiate each.

steps.title: Use the quotient rule
steps.say: The rule is $(u'v - uv')$ over $v^2$. Put in each piece.

higher.tip: Use the quotient or chain rule. Without one of them you get low partial credit at most.

sources.quote: If quotient rule or chain rule not used

higher.tip: Write the derivative out before you simplify it. The unsimplified expression earns a step of its own.
Simplify the derivative, then explain what it tells you. The explanation is a separate step.
If the answer is a fraction, leave it as a fraction. A decimal loses a mark.
